title: Zue Robertson, Jack Carroll and George Filhe: other trombonists
summary: Zue Robertson as a sweet-toned reader, Jack Carroll playing by ear, and George Filhe in marching bands.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: You were talking about Zoo Robertson? Zoo Robertson, yeah.

He was the only man, he was one of the best fellas that would go with me in bands, playing those brass band jobs, you know, like that. We played together all the time. He played first and I played second. He played on one side and I played on the other. You know, in fumes and like that. He was very good. Nice trombone player. Sweet, you know. Not a lot of harshness. He just played nice and sweet. When he had to play loud, well, he could play loud. But he always played. We'd practice that together. I used to go to his house every day and he'd come to my house. And we'd practice like that.
Was he about the same age or a little older?

Yeah, he might have been a little older than me. Because he was a settled man. He was a man when I met him. He must have been about six or seven years older than I am. But he was good. Jack Carroll, my Carroll brothers.
He's a man who played the trombone. Never knew a note. He never worried about notes. He could play, but he never worried about notes. He mostly played his music by head.
I guess Zou was a good reader. Oh, yeah.
Zou was a nice reader. He could play a little bit of piano, too. Oh, that's right. He played later in theaters.
Yeah, he could play a little bit of piano. He and his wife, I believe, traveled.
Yeah. Is that her name? Jessie?

What was the name of it? Once, I remember, even in the Defender. Wife, remember what? Had a wife and she played piano in Oregon, too. They had a job in some theater going around the country. And for a while were in West Virginia once, playing in the theater.

Yeah, he was very, very good. Nice, John Mo. That's when he was only thing about him. He liked trombone correct and everything. But he wouldn't play with a fellow if he didn't play, you know, right. You know, a man come in and played with him, played double with him, and get to blast him.
Maybe that's why some people thought he was sort of mean. Yeah. Some children come in, right.
He wouldn't have a face of a strong. Yeah, he wouldn't have a word with him. We'd talk. So that's why they say he was kind of funny, you know.
Nice, trombone correct. Yeah, I worked with him several times. George Field was good.

Yeah, I didn't get to meet him. He died about two or three years ago. Yeah, George Field. I went to his house a couple of times here. Once talked to a niece. Uh-huh. He was over at the Union playing cards that afternoon. Yeah. Before I ever got back, he was dead then. Yeah. He was very good.

Very good. Nice trombone player. I used to see him play in marches. I was rather young then when he used to play in those bands, you know. Before I got down with bands, I saw him playing in that. And they'd play marches, you know, and things like that. He was a nice trombone player. That's what I learned. And I found out that playing trombone, when you're playing and making those smears, you know, and te-de-de-de-da-da, and following up to the other instrument, I paid attention to him, watched him closely on a lot of music he played. He was good. Oh, and Joe Petit.
